chunks: The volatile keyword and when to use it. The question: What does the volatile keyword refer to? When should volatile variables be used?
volatile is a word you put on a C variable to tell the compiler: "this value can change behind your back, so look at it every time."
Compilers speed up code by remembering values instead of re-reading them. That is wrong for a variable that hardware can change, so volatile switches the shortcut off.
Imagine you check a mailbox once at 8 a. m. , see it is empty, and then write "still empty" on a sticky note. Later you just read your note, even though mail has come.
An assistant who does this to save trips is the optimizer. volatile is a sign on the mailbox saying "walk over and look every single time."
The sign forces the looking, but cannot stop the mail arriving halfway through you opening the box.
Without volatile the main loop loads the flag once into a register and keeps testing that stale copy. The ISR's write to memory is never seen, so the loop never exits.
With volatile, each iteration reloads from memory and sees the update.
Compiler / optimizer: the tool that turns your C into machine code, and the part of it that rewrites code to run faster.
Register (hardware): a special memory location that controls or reports on a device.
Interrupt / ISR: a hardware event that pauses your main code to run a short handler function at any moment. Atomic: finishes in one uninterruptible step.
Adding 1 to a variable is usually not atomic: it reads, adds, then writes.
Main code waits with while (! flag) {} . An interrupt handler sets flag to 1 when a button is pressed. The optimizer sees that nothing in the loop changes flag .
So it reads flag once, finds 0, and loops forever on that stale answer. The program hangs, but only in an optimized build.
Declare it volatile int flag; and the loop re-reads the variable on every pass. It sees the 1 and exits. That is the whole idea.
" volatile tells the compiler a variable can change outside the program's flow, or that accesses have side effects, so every read and write in the source must actually happen, in order.
Without it the optimizer can cache a flag in a register and loop forever.
I use it for memory-mapped hardware registers, variables shared between an ISR and main code, and polling loops.
But it isn't atomic, isn't a lock and isn't a memory barrier, so shared counters still need interrupts disabled or atomics."
